incidente.resumo: A new WAF Managed Rules rule for XSS detection, deployed globally, contained a regular expression that backtracked enormously and exhausted the CPU cores serving HTTP/HTTPS traffic across Cloudflare's network, so visitors to Cloudflare domains saw 502 errors and core proxying, CDN and WAF functionality went down for 27 minutes. Service returned after a global WAF termination at 14:07; the WAF was re-enabled globally at 14:52 after testing with a fix in place.

descricao.texto: Three minutes after the 13:42 deployment, a PagerDuty page from an external synthetic test indicated a fault with the WAF, rapidly followed by pages for many other failing end-to-end tests, a global traffic drop alert, widespread 502 errors and reports of CPU exhaustion from PoPs worldwide.
trechos: At 13:42 an engineer working on the firewall team deployed a minor change to the rules for XSS detection via an automatic process.
Three minutes later the first PagerDuty page went out indicating a fault with the WAF.
This was a synthetic test that checks the functionality of the WAF (we have hundreds of such tests) from outside Cloudflare to ensure that it is working correctly.

This was rapidly followed by pages indicating many other end-to-end tests of Cloudflare services failing, a global traffic drop alert, widespread 502 errors and then many reports from our points-of-presence (PoPs) in cities worldwide indicating there was CPU exhaustion.

descricao.texto: A single new WAF Managed Rules rule for XSS detection, deployed at 13:42, contained a regular expression (critical part `.*(?:.*=.*)`) that backtracked enormously and exhausted the CPU on every core handling HTTP/HTTPS traffic worldwide; front-line web servers could not reach the processes serving HTTP/HTTPS traffic and returned 502 errors.
trechos: On July 2, we deployed a new rule in our WAF Managed Rules that caused CPUs to become exhausted on every CPU core that handles HTTP/HTTPS traffic on the Cloudflare network worldwide.
At 13:42 an engineer working on the firewall team deployed a minor change to the rules for XSS detection via an automatic process.
The CPU exhaustion was caused by a single WAF rule that contained a poorly written regular expression that ended up creating excessive backtracking.
The critical part is `.*(?:.*=.*)`.
The 502 errors were generated by the front line Cloudflare web servers that still had CPU cores available but were unable to reach the processes that serve HTTP/HTTPS traffic.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: A protection that would have helped prevent excessive CPU use by a regular expression had been removed by mistake during a WAF refactoring weeks earlier, and the Lua WAF uses PCRE, a backtracking regular expression engine with no complexity guarantees and no mechanism to protect against a runaway expression.
trechos: A protection that would have helped prevent excessive CPU use by a regular expression was removed by mistake during a refactoring of the WAF weeks prior—a refactoring that was part of making the WAF use less CPU.
The regular expression engine being used didn’t have complexity guarantees.
The Lua WAF uses PCRE internally and it uses backtracking for matching and has no mechanism to protect against a runaway expression.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The CI test suite, which passed at 13:37, did not test for runaway CPU utilization by the WAF, and no increase in test suite run time was observed with the rule.
trechos: At 13:37 TeamCity built the rules and ran the tests, giving it the green light.

What it didn’t do was test for runaway CPU utilization by the WAF and examining the log files from previous WAF builds shows that no increase in test suite run time was observed with the rule that would ultimately cause CPU exhaustion on our edge.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The SOP for a rule change allowed a non-emergency change to go globally into production without a staged rollout, and WAF rules are distributed through the Quicksilver key-value store, so the change went global in seconds; the rule was meant for 'simulate' mode, but rules in simulate mode still execute.
trechos: The SOP allowed a non-emergency rule change to go globally into production without a staged rollout.
However, in this case, that speed meant that a change to the rules went global in seconds.
Because WAF rules are required to address emergent threats they are deployed using our Quicksilver distributed key-value (KV) store that can push changes globally in seconds.
This particular change was to be deployed in “simulate” mode where real customer traffic passes through the rule but nothing is blocked.
But even in the simulate mode the rules actually need to execute and in this case the rule contained a regular expression that consumed excessive CPU.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: With the Access service down, the team could not authenticate to the internal control panel or reach internal services such as Jira and the build system, and had to use an infrequently used bypass mechanism; some team members had lost access because a security feature disables credentials not used frequently on the internal control panel.
trechos: We use our own products and with our Access service down we couldn’t authenticate to our internal control panel (and once we were back we’d discover that some members of the team had lost access because of a security feature that disables their credentials if they don’t use the internal control panel frequently).
And we couldn’t get to other internal services like Jira or the build system.
To get to them we had to use a bypass mechanism that wasn’t frequently used (another thing to drill on after the event).

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The rollback plan required running the complete WAF build twice, which took too long.
trechos: The rollback plan required running the complete WAF build twice taking too long.

fatores_contribuintes.texto: The first alert for the global traffic drop took too long to fire.
trechos: The first alert for the global traffic drop took too long to fire.

descricao.texto: A new WAF Managed Rules rule targeting XSS, merged at 13:31 and automatically deployed by TeamCity at 13:42, containing the regular expression `(?:(?:\"|'|\]|\}|\\|\d|(?:nan|infinity|true|false|null|undefined|symbol|math)|\`|\-|\+)+[)]*;?((?:\s|-|~|!|{}|\|\||\+)*.*(?:.*=.*)))`.
trechos: The specific rule that caused last Tuesday’s outage was targeting Cross-site scripting (XSS) attacks.
At 13:31 an engineer on the team had merged a Pull Request containing the change after it was approved.
With the tests passing, TeamCity automatically began deploying the change at 13:42.
The regular expression that was at the heart of the outage is ``(?:(?:\"|'|\]|\}|\\|\d|(?:nan|infinity|true|false|null|undefined|symbol|math)|\`|\-|\+)+[)]*;?((?:\s|-|~|!|{}|\|\||\+)*.*(?:.*=.*)))``

passos.texto: After the WAF was identified as the cause at 14:00 and a 'global terminate' (a mechanism to disable a single component worldwide) was proposed at 14:02, a team member executed the global WAF termination at 14:07, using a bypass mechanism to reach internal systems; by 14:09 traffic levels and CPU were back to expected levels worldwide.
trechos: At 14:00 the WAF was identified as the component causing the problem and an attack dismissed as a possibility.
At 14:02 the entire team looked at me when it was proposed that we use a ‘global terminate’, a mechanism built into Cloudflare to disable a single component worldwide.
To get to them we had to use a bypass mechanism that wasn’t frequently used (another thing to drill on after the event).
Eventually, a team member executed the global WAF termination at 14:07 and by 14:09 traffic levels and CPU were back to expected levels worldwide.

acoes.texto: Already done: all release work on the WAF was stopped, and the excessive CPU usage protection that had been removed was re-introduced.
trechos: Firstly, we stopped all release work on the WAF completely and are doing the following:
Re-introduce the excessive CPU usage protection that got removed. (Done)

acoes.texto: Already done: manual inspection of all 3,868 WAF Managed Rules rules to find and correct other instances of possible excessive backtracking (inspection complete).
trechos: Manually inspecting all 3,868 rules in the WAF Managed Rules to find and correct any other instances of possible excessive backtracking. (Inspection complete)

acoes.texto: Introduce performance profiling for all rules to the test suite (ETA July 19).
trechos: Introduce performance profiling for all rules to the test suite. (ETA:  July 19)

acoes.texto: Switch to either the re2 or Rust regex engine, both of which have run-time guarantees (ETA July 31); in the longer term, port the WAF away from the Lua WAF to the new firewall engine.
trechos: Switching to either the re2 or Rust regex engine which both have run-time guarantees. (ETA: July 31)
In the longer term we are moving away from the Lua WAF that I wrote years ago. We are porting the WAF to use the new firewall engine.

acoes.texto: Change the SOP to do staged rollouts of rules in the same manner as other Cloudflare software, while retaining the ability to do emergency global deployment for active attacks.
trechos: Changing the SOP to do staged rollouts of rules in the same manner used for other software at Cloudflare while retaining the ability to do emergency global deployment for active attacks.

acoes.texto: Put in place an emergency ability to take the Cloudflare Dashboard and API off Cloudflare's edge, and automate updates of the Cloudflare Status page.
trechos: Putting in place an emergency ability to take the Cloudflare Dashboard and API off Cloudflare's edge.
Automating update of the Cloudflare Status page.

Although the regular expression itself is of interest to many people (and is discussed more below), the real story of how the Cloudflare service went down for 27 minutes is much more complex than “a regular expression went bad”.
